title: What Is a Higgs Boson Actually Made Of… And Why Does Mass Depend on It?
fullText: Tonight, we're going to go inside the smallest thing physicists have ever found and ask a question that almost no one thinks to ask. Not what the Higs Bzon does and not where it came from, but what it's actually made of. Because here's the thing most people don't realize. The Higs Bzon, the particle that supposedly gives everything in the universe its mass, the particle that took 50 years and the largest machine ever built to find might not be fundamental at all. It might have structure. It might have parts. And if it does, everything we think we know about why matter exists, why you exist, needs to be rebuilt from the ground up. By the end of tonight, you're going to understand not just what the Higs Bzon is, but why the question of what it's made of might be the most important question in all of physics. Before we begin, if you enjoy these topics as much as we do, make sure to like the video or subscribe. It's a simple action, but it helps this channel reach more curious minds like yours. Now, let's begin. There is a field that fills all of space. Every cubic cm of the universe, from the emptiest void between galaxies to the interior of your own body, is threaded through by something invisible. You can't see it. You can't feel it directly. There is no instrument that can point at it and say, "Here it is." But without it, nothing would have mass. Electrons, quarks, the building blocks of every atom in every star in every galaxy would be completely massless. They would race through the universe at the speed of light, never slowing, never binding together, never forming the structures we call matter. There would be no atoms, no moleculars, no chemistry, no planets, no you. This field is called the Higs field and it is in a very real sense the reason anything exists the way it exists. The Higs Bzon is what physicists call an excitation of that field. When you pour enough energy into the Higs field in a small enough region of space, you disturb it. And that disturbance takes the form of a particle, a ripple in something that is otherwise perfectly still. That particle is the Higs Bzon. And on the 4th of July 2012, after searching for it for nearly 50 years, physicists found it. The announcement came from CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research on the Swiss French border outside Geneva. Both major detector collaborations at the Large Hadron Collider, Atlas and CMS, announced a discovery simultaneously. It was one of the most significant moments in the history of science. The crowd in the auditorium included Peter Higgs himself, the British physicist who had first proposed the mechanism in 1964. He was 83 years old. When the result was announced, he was seen wiping tears from his eyes. He had spent nearly half a century waiting for this confirmation. But here is where the story gets complicated. The discovery of the Higs Bzon was not the end of something. It was the beginning of an entirely different set of questions. Because the moment physicists actually had a Higs Bzon to study, they began measuring it. Its mass, its spin, the ways it decays into other particles, the rates at which those decays happen. And some of those measurements came back almost exactly right, almost exactly as predicted, almost, but not quite. And in physics, almost is a very interesting word. The standard model of particle physics is the most successful scientific theory ever written down. It describes with extraordinary precision the behavior of all known fundamental particles and the forces that govern them with one major exception we'll come back to. It predicted the existence of particles decades before experiments could find them. It made numerical predictions accurate to more than 10 decimal places. When the theory says an electron's magnetic moment should be 2.0 2319 30 436 and you measure it and get exactly that, you start to trust the theory. The standard model is built on a framework called quantum field theory. The basic idea is that space is not empty. It is filled with fields. Every type of particle corresponds to a field that permeates all of space. An electron is an excitation of the electron field. A photon is an excitation of the electromagnetic field. A quark is an excitation of a quark field. And the Higs Bzon is an excitation of the Higs field. These fields interact with each other according to rules that can be written down as precise mathematical equations. The interactions produce what we observe as forces. Electromagnetism, the weak nuclear force, the strong nuclear force. The standard model describes all of these beautifully. It does not describe gravity. That is the exception. General relativity handles gravity and the two frameworks quantum field theory and general relativity have so far refused to be unified into a single consistent description. That problem is real, enormous, and separate from what we are discussing here. But within its domain, the standard model is a machine that simply works. The Higs field occupies a unique position within it. The other fields in the standard model acquire their properties from the mathematics of the theory. The photon is massless because of a symmetry in the equations. The gluon is massless for a related reason, but the Higs field is different. The Higs field has what's called a nonzero vacuum expectation value. That is a technical phrase with a very specific meaning. It means that even in its lowest energy state, even when the universe is as calm and empty as it can be, the Higsfield does not sit at zero. It sits at a specific nonzero value, like a ball at the top of a perfectly symmetric hill that has rolled off to one side and settled there. The exact value it settles at is 246 ga electron volts. And that nonzero value is what breaks the symmetry of the standard model. It is what allows particles to have mass. This mechanism is called electroeak symmetry breaking. It is one of the most elegant pieces of physics ever discovered. To understand what the Higsfield actually does, you need to understand what mass means at a fundamental level. Because mass is not what most people think it is. When you pick up a rock and feel its weight, you are feeling two things. Gravity pulling on the rock and the rock's resistance to being moved. What physicists call inertia. Both of these are related to mass, but neither one is mass itself. Mass at its deepest level is a measure of how strongly a particle interacts with the Higs field. Particles that interact strongly with the Higs field have high mass. Particles that interact weakly have low mass. And particles like the photon that don't interact with the Higs field at all are completely massless. The technical term for this interaction is a yukawa coupling. Each type of fundamental particle has its own coupling strength to the Higs field. The top quark, the heaviest known fundamental particle, has a yukawa coupling close to one. That means it interacts with the Higs field about as strongly as it possibly can. The electron has a coupling of about 3 * 10 ^ of -6. It interacts with the Higs field only faintly. That is why the top quark is about 339,000 times more massive than the electron. Not because they are made of different stuff in any obvious sense, but because they couple to the Higs field in very different ways. These coupling values are put into the standard model by hand. The theory does not predict them. It accommodates them. You measure the mass of each particle. You calculate its coupling constant and you write it in. Physicists call numbers like these free parameters. There are about 20 such parameters in the standard model. They are measured not derived. And that bothers physicists deeply because a truly fundamental theory should explain why those numbers are what they are, not just accept them as inputs. A theory that simply accommodates every measurement without explaining any of them is in a sense not a theory at all. It is a catalog. The standard model, as magnificent as it is, is partly a catalog. And the Higs sector is where that limitation is most visible. The coupling of the electron to the Higs field is about 340,000 times smaller than the coupling of the top quark to the Higsfield. No one knows why. It is what it is, written in, accepted, not explained. That gap in understanding is where new physics must eventually live. Now we arrive at the real question. What is the Higs Bzon made of? In the standard model, the honest answer is nothing. It is a fundamental particle pointlike structureless with no internal components. like an electron or a quark. It is one of the basic ingredients of reality, not assembled from anything smaller. But here's why that answer is deeply unsatisfying. The Higs Bzon has a mass of approximately 125.25 giga electron volts. A giga electron volt or GEV is a unit of energy used in particle physics where energy and mass are interchangeable through E= MC². 125 GEV means the Higs Bzon is about 133 times heavier than a proton. For reference, a proton has a mass of about 0.938 GEV. So the Higs is heavy. Not the heaviest particle. The top quark at about 173 GEV takes that prize. But solidly in the high end of the mass spectrum. And that mass creates a problem, a deep uncomfortable problem called the hierarchy problem. Here is how it works. In quantum field theory, every particle interacts with every other particle through quantum fluctuations. Virtual particles pop in and out of existence everywhere in space, even in total vacuum. These fluctuations are not hypothetical. They produce measurable effects on real particles. The Casemir effect, where two uncharged metal plates placed very close together are pushed toward each other by vacuum fluctuations of the electromagnetic field, is one of the cleanest demonstrations that quantum fluctuations are physically real. They measured it in the lab. The force is there. The vacuum is not empty. It is seething with quantum activity. These fluctuations contribute to the physical properties of particles including their mass. The technical term is radiative corrections. When you calculate the Higs mass by summing up all the contributions from all these quantum fluctuations, you get a number that is almost infinitely large, far larger than what we measure. Specifically, the corrections push the Higs mass toward the highest energy scale in the problem. In particle physics, the most natural high energy scale is the plank scale. the energy at which quantum gravitational effects become important. The plank scale is about 10 ^ of 19 gev 1 followed by 19 zeros in units of giga electron volts. The higs mass is about 125 gev. The ratio of the observed higs mass to the plank scale is roughly 10 ^ of -17. To get a sensible answer out of the calculation, something has to cancel those corrections almost perfectly. The technical word for this precise cancellation is finetuning. The degree of fine-tuning required to get the Higs mass right is approximately one part in 10 to the power of 34. 10 to the power of 34. One followed by 34 zeros. Physicists call this the hierarchy problem and it is one of the most uncomfortable facts in modern physics because fine-tuning at that level does not happen by accident in nature. When you see a balance that precise, your first instinct is that something is keeping it in place. There is a mechanism. There is a reason. The question is what? And the answer to that question almost certainly involves the Higs Bzon being something more than a structurous point. Before we go into what that something more might be, it helps to understand the historical precedent. Because the hierarchy problem is not the first time physicists have encountered an uncomfortable sensitivity of this kind. And the solution has never been fine-tuning. It has always been new structure. In the 1960s, the proton was considered fundamental. It was on the list of basic building blocks of matter along with the electron, the neutron, and a growing zoo of other particles being discovered in accelerators around the world. The proton was where physics stopped. Below the proton, nothing. Then experiments at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center in California in 1967 and 1968 began revealing something unexpected. Physicists fired high energy electrons at protons and watched how the electrons scattered. At low energies, the electrons scattered off the whole proton as if hitting a small featureless ball. But at higher energies, the scattering pattern changed fundamentally. The electrons were bouncing off of individual point-like objects inside the proton, not the proton as a whole, something smaller. Those objects are what we now call quarks. The proton is not fundamental. It is made of three quarks bound together by a new force. The strong nuclear force mediated by particles called gluons. This was one of the defining discoveries of 20th century physics. James Bjorkan worked out the theoretical framework for understanding the scattering at high energies. Richard Fineman contributed the parton model interpretation. Murray Galman and George Zv had independently proposed quarks as mathematical objects in 1964 before any direct evidence for them existed. The deep inelastic scattering experiments at Stanford confirmed that the quarks were real physical objects inside the proton. The proton dissolved conceptually into something smaller and more fundamental. This pattern of looking inside something we thought was fundamental and finding structure has repeated itself throughout the history of physics. Atoms into nuclei and electrons. Nuclei into protons and neutrons, protons and neutrons into quarks. The Higs Bzon is the next candidate. And the hierarchy problem is the theoretical hint that the pattern might be about to repeat. Something is wrong with the Higs at the level of the standard model alone. Something needs to fix it. And the most historically consistent fix is new structure. There are several serious proposals for what might resolve the hierarchy problem. The first and most famous is super symmetry. Super symmetry is a proposed symmetry between two fundamentally different types of particles. In the standard model, particles come in two varieties. Firmians, particles with half integer spin like quarks and electrons. The matter particles and bzons, particles with integer spin like photons and gluons, the force carrying particles. The Higs Bzon is also a Bzon with spin zero. Super symmetry proposes that every firmion has a bzonic super partner and every Bzon has a firmionic super partner. The electron has a super partner called the selectron. The quarks have super partners called squarks. The gluon has a super partner called the gluino. The Higs Bzon has fionic super partners called Higinos. These super partners have not been observed. If they existed at low energies, we would have found them by now. But they might exist at higher energies than current colliders can reach. The reason super symmetry was originally exciting beyond being mathematically elegant is that in a super symmetric theory the quantum corrections to the Higs mass cancel exactly. Every contribution from a standard model particle to the Higs mass is precisely canled by the contribution from its super partner. Firmian loops and Bzon loops contribute with opposite signs. In a super symmetric theory, those opposite sign contributions cancel perfectly. The hierarchy problem disappears, not by accident, but by symmetry. A beautiful resolution. But super symmetry does not resolve the question of what the Higs is made of. In super symmetry, the Higs Bzon is still fundamental, still structureless, still pointlike, still an elementary degree of freedom. Super symmetry solves the hierarchy problem without answering the compositess question, which is why it has always coexisted with other proposals that take a more radical step. That more radical step is the idea that the Higs Bzon is not fundamental at all. That it is a composite particle assembled from smaller, more fundamental constituents held together by a new force. This idea has a name, compositess, and it has the historical precedent we just discussed. If the Higs is composite, if it is assembled from smaller constituents, then its mass is set naturally by the energy scale of whatever new force binds those constituents together. No fine-tuning required. The mass of a proton is not finetuned. It emerges naturally from the dynamics of the strong force that binds its quarks. The proton mass of about 0.938 Gev is set by the energy scale at which the strong force becomes strong enough to confine quarks into bound states. That energy scale is called the QCD confinement scale around 200MEV. The proton mass is of the same order. A composite Higs could work the same way. If there is a new force, something analogous to QCD, but operating at a higher energy scale, and if that force confines new fundamental particles into a bound state, the mass of that bound state would be naturally of order of the confinement scale. You would not need fine tuning to explain why the Higs mass is much smaller than the plank scale. The Higs mass would be determined by the confinement scale of the new force. And if that confinement scale is a few TV, a few terra electron volts, the Higs mass would naturally come out around the electroeak scale around 100 GV close to what we observe. The hierarchy problem is not solved by cancellation as in super symmetry. It is solved by natural dynamics by the same mechanism that gives the proton its mass. No tuning, no special choice of parameters, just the physics of confinement. The most developed composite Higs framework historically is called Technicolor. Proposed in the late 1970s by Leonard Suskin at Stanford and independently by Steven Weinberg at Harvard. Technicolor was a bold reimagining of electroeak symmetry breaking. Instead of a fundamental scalar Higs field, you have a new force, the technicolor force and new fundamental particles called technifirmians. The technical force is a scaled up version of QCD. Just as QCD confines quarks into protons and pions, the technical force confines technians into bound states at a higher energy scale. And just as the pion of QCD is a pseudo Namboo Goldstone Bzon, a particle whose existence is tied to a broken approximate symmetry. The wouldbe Higs Bzon in Technicolor is a bound state of technifirm pairs. Electroeak symmetry would be broken by the condensation of technifirmian pairs in the vacuum similar to how superconductors form Kooper pairs of electrons. No fundamental scalar field needed. No fundamental higs bzon. Just bound states of technapirmians produced by a new force. It was a beautiful idea. Elegant in exactly the way physicists hope their theories will be. And it mostly does not work. Original technical models ran into severe problems with precision measurements of electroeak observables. The W and Zed Bzans had been discovered at CERN in 1983 by Carlo Rubia and Simon Vaneir's team, confirming a key prediction of the electroeak theory. After the discovery, precision measurements of the W and Z masses and their interaction rates became powerful probes of new physics. The S parameter and T parameter are two combinations of measured electroeak quantities that constrain how strongly any new physics can affect the electroeak sector. Early technical models predicted values for these parameters that conflicted with measurements from the large electron positron collider at CERN in the 1990s. The simplest versions were ruled out. What followed was a period of intense theoretical work trying to save the basic idea by making it more sophisticated. Walking technicol proposed a technical force with different behavior at different energy scales chosen to reduce the problematic corrections. Top color models added a new strong force specifically for the top quark addressing its unusually large mass separately. Top Technicolor combined these ideas into unified frameworks. Each variation addressed specific problems and introduced new ones. The theoretical landscape became complicated. Some versions remained viable, but then the Higs Bzon was discovered in 2012 with a mass of about 125 GEV. And that complicated things further because a fully composite Higs made entirely of technifirmians would generally produce couplings to other particles that deviate significantly from standard model predictions. the deviations would be of order one meaning roughly 100% difference in some coupling that is not what was measured. The measured couplings are close to standard model values. So if the Higs is composite, it is a very particular kind of composite, one that mimics an elementary particle extremely well, one that requires a more subtle theoretical framework than simple technicolor. This is where the most interesting modern frameworks come in. Composite Higs models with a pseudo Namboo Goldstone Bzon structure. The key concept is a pseudo namboo gold stone bzon. To understand what that is, you need to understand Emmy Noathther. Emmy Noithther was a German mathematician working in the early 20th century. In 1915, she proved a theorem that turned out to be one of the cornerstones of modern physics. Noeth's theorem states that every continuous symmetry of a physical system corresponds to a conserved quantity. If a system is symmetric under rotation in space, angular momentum is conserved. If it is symmetric under translation in time, meaning the laws of physics are the same yesterday as today, energy is conserved. If it is symmetric under translation in space, momentum is conserved. These are not coincidences. They are deep mathematical connections between symmetry and conservation. The reverse also has profound implications. When a continuous symmetry is spontaneously broken, meaning the equations respect the symmetry, but the actual ground state of the system does not, something remarkable happens. Massless particles appear. These are called Namboo Goldstone Bzons, named after Yoiro Namboo, who received the Nobel Prize in physics in 2008 for related ideas. and Jeffrey Goldstone who formalized the theorem in 1961. The pions the particles that mediate interactions between protons and neutrons in the nucleus are the best known example in particle physics. The equations describing the strong force have an approximate symmetry called chyal symmetry. When the strong force confines quarks into hadrons at low energies, that chyal symmetry is spontaneously broken. The pions are the namboo gold stone bzons of that breaking because the symmetry is only approximate, not exact. The pions are not exactly massless. They are light compared to the proton and other hadrons, but they are not zero. They are pseudo namboo goldstone bzons pseudo because the symmetry that produced them is only approximate. The composite Higs models propose something similar for the Higs itself. There is a new strong force at a higher energy scale. This force is governed by a symmetry group. When the interaction confines new constituents at some energy scale, it spontaneously breaks a larger symmetry group down to a smaller subgroup. The Higs Bzon emerges as a pseudo Namboo Goldstone Bzon of that broken symmetry. Because it is a pseudo Namboo Goldstone Bzon, its mass is protected by the approximate symmetry. Quantum corrections to its mass are suppressed. no fine tuning and because the symmetry is only approximate the Higs mass is non zero but naturally much smaller than the compositess scale. The ratio of the Higs mass to the compositess scale is calculable from the dynamics. No arbitrary numbers inserted by hand. This is why these models are taken seriously. They offer a genuine mechanism for why the Higs mass is what it is. Not an accident, not fine-tuning, a consequence of structure. The simplest composite Higs model is built on the co-et space. So SO5 over SO4. So5 is the special orthogonal group in five dimensions. a mathematical object describing rotations in fivedimensional space. SO4 is the same object for four dimensions. The notation SO5 over SO4 describes the mathematical space that remains when the larger symmetry group is broken to its subgroup. The mathematics of this symmetry breaking produces exactly four Namboo Goldstone bosoms. Three of them get absorbed by the weak forces W and Zed bosans giving those particles their mass. This is the same mechanism as in the standard model but now the Higs is a bound state rather than a fundamental field. The fourth Namboo Goldstone Bzon is what we call the Higs Bzon. The appeal of this construction is that the ratio of the Higs vacuum expectation value to the compositess scale, usually called XI, controls how much the Higs deviates from elementary particle behavior. When XI is small, meaning the Higs vacuum expectation value is much smaller than the compositness scale, the Higs looks almost exactly like an elementary particle. Current measurements from the Large Hadron Collider constrain XI to be no larger than about 0.1 10%. The compositness scale is therefore at least several TV above the energy of current LHC runs. That is why we haven't seen the constituents yet. They are hiding just above where we can look. Like the quarks inside the proton before the Stanford accelerator could reach the energy needed to see them scatter individually. Now the question of what those constituents actually are. In analogy with the proton, they would be something like quarks for the Higs field. Physicists call them by various names depending on the model. Pons is a generic term for hypothetical subcomponents of quarks and lepttons. In composite Higs contexts, the bound states are sometimes called hyperquarks or technifirmians if the binding force resembles QCD. What these constituents have in common across most models is that they carry charges under a new force. This new force acts similarly to the strong nuclear force but at a higher energy scale. The strong nuclear force is described by QCD quantum chromodnamics. Its coupling strength is large at low energies, which is why quarks are confined inside protons and can't escape individually. At high energies, the coupling becomes smaller. Individual quarks behave almost freely inside a very fast collision. This property is called astoic freedom and it was discovered in 1973 by David Gross, Frank Wilchek and David Pulitzer who received the Nobel Prize in physics for it in 2004. The hypothetical force binding Higs constituents would have the same qualitative behavior. At energies above the compositness scale, you would see the constituents moving freely. At lower energies, they would be confined into bound states like the Higs Bzon. The nature of those bound states would determine the entire spectrum of particles. The model predicts not just the Higs Bzon but a whole family of heavier particles analogous to the heavier maison and barons above the pion in the QCD spectrum. The rows the omega meons the Eater prime all part of the bound state spectrum of the strong force. The composite Higs would come with an analogous spectrum. Heavier vector resonances at the te scale. Firmionic partners of the Higs constituents. New scalar particles beyond just the one we found. These are the signatures that particle physicists search for at the large hadron collider and so far they have not been found. But the search is ongoing and the limits being placed on these particles are pushing the models into more constrained parameter regions which is progress. Even the absence of a signal is information. The large hadron collider has collected an enormous amount of data. Its two main experiments, Atlas and CMS, each hold data sets from run one, run two, and run three. The LHC ran at a center of mass energy of 13TV in run two, and 13.6 TV in run three. The analyses of the Higs couplings from those data sets are remarkably precise. The coupling of the Higs to bottom quarks to tow leptons to W bzons to Z bzons to top quarks to photons all have been measured and all of them agree with standard model predictions to within a few percent. Some even to within 1 or 2%. This tight agreement is both reassuring and frustrating. Reassuring because the theory works, frustrating because there is no sign yet of what lies beneath. If the Higs is composite at the few TV scale, there should be deviations. Small ones of order sigh, but detectable. Some analyses see small hints, a 2% excess here, a 1% deficit there. But none of these are significant enough to claim as new physics. They could easily be statistical fluctuations. They could be systematic effects not perfectly accounted for. Physicists are careful about this. You do not claim a discovery until the evidence reaches five sigma. Meaning the probability of a statistical fluctuation producing that signal is less than 1 in 3 12 million. Current hints in Higs coupling measurements are nowhere near five sigma. So the status right now is the Higs looks elementary but the precision of our measurements is not yet sharp enough to rule out a composite nature at the level predicted by the best composite Higs models. The high luminosity LHC upgrade is expected to change this. The HLHC, scheduled to begin operations in the early 2030s, will collect about 10 times more data than all previous LHC runs combined. That data will allow HIGS coupling measurements with per mill precision, meaning a few tenths of a percent. If the Higs is composite with XI at the level of 5% or larger, the HL LHC should see it. If it does not, that pushes the compositess scale to higher energies and she to smaller values. It makes composite models more constrained, but does not rule them out. There are also proposals for future colliders that would go further. The future circular collider or FCC would have a circumference of about 91 km almost 3 and a half times the size of the LHC which sits in a tunnel 27 km in circumference beneath the Swiss French border. The FCC in its first phase as an electron posetron collider called FCCE would produce millions of Higs bosons in very clean conditions. Electron posetron collisions are cleaner than proton proton collisions because electrons and posetrons are fundamental particles. When they collide, you know exactly what went into the collision. With proton proton collisions, you are really colliding quarks and gluons and you have to account for the internal structure of the proton. That introduces uncertainties that limit precision. FCCE would improve precision on Higs couplings by another factor of 5 to 10 beyond the HLHC. The second phase of the FCC as a proton proton collider at 100TV called FCCHH would then push into entirely new energy territory. The circular electron posetron collider proposed in China, the CPC would do similar things to FCCE. All of these proposals are motivated substantially by the need to understand the Higs Bzon at a deeper level. The stakes are high enough that multiple countries are willing to spend tens of billions on the infrastructure needed to study this one particle more carefully. That tells you something about how important the question is. There is another angle to the compositess question that goes beyond just measuring Higs couplings. If the Higs is composite, then at some high energy, you can resolve its internal structure. You can see the constituents. You can scatter off of them individually. This is exactly what the deep inelastic scattering experiments did for the proton in the 1960s. Fire a particle at a proton with enough energy and instead of it bouncing off the whole proton, it bounces off an individual quark inside. The pattern of the scattering tells you how many quarks there are, what their charges are, how fast they are moving around inside the proton. The same principle applies to a composite Higs. At energies above the compositess scale, you would no longer produce a single Higs Bzon in the usual way. You would instead produce pairs or groups of the fundamental constituents directly. Their interactions would be described not by the Higsfield equations but by the new strong force that binds them and the scattering patterns in colliders would change completely. A future collider at 100 TV of center of mass energy could potentially reach compositess scales of tens of TV. If the Higs is composite at that scale, the FCC-H might not just measure deviations in Higs couplings. It might directly produce the constituents. See the Higs dissolve into its components at high energy. Just as the proton dissolves into quarks and gluons when you hit it hard enough, that would be the definitive answer. Not a deviation, not a hint, but direct observation of the structure inside the Higs, the particle physics equivalent of watching the proton come apart for the first time. There is another class of ideas that deserves careful attention. Extra dimensions. In the late 1990s, several groups of physicists realized that if there are additional spatial dimensions beyond the three we experience, some of the most puzzling features of particle physics could be explained geometrically. The most developed framework of this kind comes from Lisa Randall and Ramen Sundrum. Their 1999 papers proposed that the universe has a fifth dimension that is curved in a specific way. The geometry is called anti-deitter space. It is a five-dimensional space with a negative cosmological constant. In this picture, there are two fourdimensional surfaces called brains separated along the fifth dimension. Gravity is concentrated near one brain called the plank brain. The standard model fields including the Higs live on the other brain called the Tevy brain. The gravitational field spreads through the fifth dimension. But its amplitude decays exponentially as you move away from the plank brain toward the TEV brain. By the time you reach the te brain, the effective plank scale, the energy at which gravity becomes strong has been exponentially suppressed. A modest extra dimension can produce an exponential hierarchy. The plank scale of 10 to the power of 19 Gev gets mapped to a TV scale by this exponential warp factor. The hierarchy problem is resolved geometrically. no fine-tuning of parameters. The smallness of the Higs mass compared to the plank mass is a consequence of the geometry of the extra dimension. In these models, the Higs Bzon can be identified with a component of the gauge field in the extra dimension. A five-dimensional gauge field has five components. Four of them behave like a standard four-dimensional gauge field. The fifth component pointing along the extra dimension becomes a four-dimensional scalar field when the extra dimension is compactified. This is called gauge Higs unification. The Higs Bzon is in this picture the fifth component of a fivedimensional vector Bzon. In this sense, the Higs has structure in an extradimensional sense. It is composite in the extra dimension. Even if it appears elementary in the four dimensions we directly probe the masses of the kooa klein excitations heavier copies of standard model particles that arise from the extradimensional nature of the fields would appear at the te scale. Atlas and CMS have searched extensively for Kuzacleine gravitons and kousacle gauge bosoms. Mass limits of several TEV have been placed on the lightest resonances. The simplest Randall Sundrum models are constrained. More complicated versions with additional ingredients to suppress dangerous processes remain allowed and actively studied. The connection between extra dimensions and composite models is not just analogical. In 1997, one Maldesina proposed something extraordinary, a mathematical duality between two completely different types of theories. On one side, a quantum field theory in four dimensions with no gravity. On the other side, a gravitational theory in five dimensions with a negative cosmological constant anti-deitter space. The claim is that these two theories describe the same physics. They are dual to each other. A calculation in the fourdimensional field theory corresponds to a calculation in the fivedimensional gravitational theory. This duality is called the anti-deitter conformal field theory correspondence or ads CFT. It has been one of the most fertile ideas in theoretical physics for the last three decades. What does this have to do with the Higs Bzon? Randall Sundum extradimensional models are through this correspondence dual to composite field theories. The Kuza Klein excitations of the extradimensional model correspond to the bound states of the composite theory. The warp factor of the extradimension corresponds to the running of the coupling in the new strong force. This means that composite Higs models and extradimensional models are not just analogous. They are related by a precise mathematical duality. If you solve the composite model, you get the same answer as solving the extradimensional model. They are different descriptions of the same underlying physics. This duality makes composite Higs models more tractable. Calculations that are difficult in the strongly coupled four-dimensional theory become calculable in the weakly curved five-dimensional gravitational theory. And it has deepened the theoretical understanding of what compositess means. In a sense, asking whether the Higs is composite is asking whether there is a higher dimensional description of reality where the extra dimension encodes the internal structure of what we see as an elementary particle in four dimensions. A different framing but the same experimental predictions, the same vector resonances, the same firmionic partners, the same deviations in Higs couplings because the physics is the same regardless of which description you use to calculate it. There is yet another framework that has received significant attention in the last two decades. The twin higs mechanism proposed around 2005 by Zakaria Chako Hawken Go and Rooney Hanik. The actual process of measuring the Higs Bzon is more intricate than most people realize. The Higs Bzon is produced in the collisions at the LHC, but it doesn't live long enough to travel any macroscopic distance. Its lifetime is about 1.6 6 * 10 to the power of -22 seconds. That is fantastically short. In that time, traveling at close to the speed of light, the Higs moves less than 110,000th of a millimeter before it decays. So, you never see the Higs Bzon directly. You see the particles it decays into. And then you work backward to figure out that a Higs Bzon was there. The Higs has several major decay modes. The most common about 58% of the time is decay into a pair of bottom quarks. The bottom quark and its antiparticle are produced together. But bottom quarks are difficult to detect cleanly because the LHC produces enormous numbers of quark pairs through other processes. The bottom quark decay channel was only observed with high significance in 2018, 6 years after the initial discovery. The second most common decay about 22% of the time is into a pair of W bosons. But one of the W bosons is offshell, meaning it doesn't have enough energy to be a real W boson. This makes the reconstruction complicated. About 2.6% of the time, the Higs decays into a pair of Z bzons. This is the golden channel because both Z bosons can decay into pairs of leptons, electrons, or muons. These are clean signals in the detector, easy to identify. The original discovery was largely based on the decay into two Z bzons decaying into four lepttons and the decay into two photons which happens only about 0.2% of the time. Very rare, but photons are exquisitly well measured in the detector. The two photon decay channel was one of the two key channels for the initial discovery. Each of these decay modes is sensitive to different aspects of the Higs couplings. The decay to bottom quarks measures the coupling to bottom quarks. The decay to W bosans measures the coupling to W bosons. The decay to two photons involves loops of top quarks and W bzons. So it is sensitive to the coupling to top quarks as well. By measuring all of these rates and comparing them to standard model predictions, you get the complete picture of the Higs couplings and any deviation in any channel is a potential signal of new physics. This is why Higs coupling measurements are so central to the search for physics beyond the standard model. They are not just interesting for their own sake. They are probes of everything that could be interacting with the Higs, including whatever the Higs might be made of. There is one more aspect of the Higs Bzon that deserves attention. The question of whether it is stable, not in the sense of how long it lives before decaying. We know that about 10 to the^ of -22 seconds. But in the sense of whether the Higs field itself, the background field that permeates all of space is in a stable state or a metastable one. This is a question about the vacuum of the universe. The vacuum is not empty. It is a state of the Higs field sitting at its minimum value of 246 GEV. But the shape of the Higs potential at very high field values depends on quantum corrections from the top quark and other particles. And those corrections calculated within the standard model using the measured value of the top quark mass and the Higs mass suggest something disturbing. At very high field values far larger than 246 GEV, the Higs potential may develop another deeper minimum. If that deeper minimum exists, then the vacuum we live in is not the true vacuum. It is a false vacuum, a metastable state that could in principle decay to the true vacuum. This decay would proceed by quantum tunneling. A bubble of true vacuum would nucleate somewhere in space and expand at the speed of light. Inside the bubble, the laws of physics would be different. The Higs vacuum expectation value would have a different value. Particles would have different masses. Chemistry as we know it would not work. This process, if it happened, would be completely invisible until the bubble wall arrived at your location and it would arrive at the speed of light. So there would be no warning. Now, the good news is that calculations suggest the vacuum is either stable or extremely longived. The lifetime of a metastable vacuum is estimated to be vastly longer than the current age of the universe. So there is no practical concern. But the question of whether we live in a stable or metastable vacuum is a deep one and the answer depends sensitively on the exact values of the top quark mass and the Higs mass. The current measurements of both sit very close to the boundary between stability and meta stability. It is not clear which side we are on. Some calculations say stable, some say metastable. The uncertainties in the top quark mass are large enough that we can't be certain. Better measurements of both the top quark mass and the Higs mass are needed. And more importantly, a deeper understanding of the Higs potential at high field values, which requires knowing what the Higs is made of. Because if the Higs is composite, its potential at high field values is completely different from the elementary Higs potential. The question of vacuum stability is yet another reason why understanding the structure of the Higs field matters. Not just for particle physics, but for the ultimate fate of the universe. The searches at Atlas and CMS continue. analyses of run. Three data from the LHC are ongoing. Teams of hundreds of physicists pour over the data looking for deviations, excesses, anomalies. Anything that does not fit the standard model, anything that might be a signal of what lies beneath. And when they finish with run three, there will be the high luminosity upgrade. And after that the debate about future colliders. Every one of those future machines is at its core a machine for asking the same question. What is the Higs Bzon made of? The answer when it comes will tell us whether there are new forces in nature, new constituents of matter, new dimensions of space or some mechanism for naturalness that no one has thought of yet. It will be one of the great discoveries in the history of science. Or it will be the absence of a discovery which would force an even deeper rethinking of what we understand about the universe. Either outcome changes everything. And either outcome will be the result of experiment, of data, of measurements made by machines built over decades, by thousands of physicists in dozens of countries, working on one of the oldest questions in human inquiry. What is matter made of at the deepest level we can reach? The Higs Bosson is the current frontier of that question and we are standing at it right now. Before we talk about where this search is ultimately heading, it helps to understand how particle physics actually works as a scientific enterprise because it is different from almost every other field of science. A particle physics experiment at the LHC is not designed, run, and analyzed by a single team. The Atlas detector is operated by a collaboration of thousands of physicists from more than 180 institutions in around 38 countries. The CMS detector has a similar collaboration. These are not small research groups. They are distributed international organizations with a complexity comparable to a small country's scientific infrastructure. When Atlas publishes a result, it carries the names of thousands of authors. Every significant analysis goes through multiple rounds of internal review before it reaches the public. This might sound bureaucratic. It is, but it is also a quality control system of extraordinary rigor. A result that has survived internal scrutiny by 5,000 physicists is a result that has been stress tested in ways that smaller experiments cannot match. The flip side is that particle physics operates on long time scales. The LHC took decades to design and build. The Atlas and CMS detectors were themselves massive engineering projects spanning 15 years of construction. When physicists talk about the HLLHC upgrade, they are talking about an upgrade that will take most of the 1920s to install and commission. When they talk about the FCC, they are talking about a machine that would begin operations perhaps in the 1950s. These are time scales that exceed individual careers. Most of the physicists currently working on the conceptual design of the FCC will not be alive when it produces its first results. This is a long game and it requires a kind of institutional commitment that is rare in human endeavors. The question of what the Higs Bzon is made of might not be answered in the professional lifetime of any person currently working on it. It might be answered in the lifetimes of graduate students who are just starting their careers today. Or it might be answered by their students. The search has its own time scale determined not by what physicists want but by what nature requires. There is a deeper philosophical point embedded in everything we have discussed. When physicists ask what is the Higs Bzon made of, they are asking whether there is a more fundamental level of description of reality than the one we currently have. Every time we have asked this question in the history of physics, the answer has been yes. Atoms are made of nuclei and electrons. Nuclei are made of protons and neutrons. Protons and neutrons are made of quarks. Each step revealed a new layer of structure, a new force governing that structure, a new set of constituents. Each step required new machines and new theoretical frameworks. Each step changed our understanding of what matter is. There is no known reason why the quarks and lepttons of the standard model should be the final layer. There is no theorem that says the descent into structure must stop here. The theoretical arguments, particularly the hierarchy problem, actively suggest it doesn't stop here. And the historical pattern says it probably doesn't stop here. But we don't know. We genuinely don't know whether there is structure below the quarks. We don't know whether there is structure inside the higs. We are asking the question and we are waiting for nature to answer. That is the honest position. And it is a position worth sitting with because it means we are at a frontier, a real frontier, not a metaphorical one. The edge of what is known. And the question on the other side of that edge, the question of what the Higs Bzon is actually made of might be one of the most fundamental questions a human mind has ever asked. It is asking what reality is made of at its smallest scale and we don't know the answer yet. But we have the tools and the will to find out. The story of how the Higs Bzon was predicted is itself remarkable. In 1964, three groups of physicists working independently published papers describing essentially the same mechanism. Robert Bout and Francois Englet in Brussels, Peter Higgs in Edinburgh, Gerald Geralnik, Carl Hagen and Tom Kibble in London. All three papers appeared within a few months of each other. All three described how a scalar field could break gauge symmetry and give mass to gauge bzans. The mechanism is now called the boutinglet Higs mechanism in some contexts and the Higs mechanism in others. The particle it predicts is called the Higs Bzon after Peter Higgs who specifically emphasized in his paper that there should be a massive scalar particle associated with the symmetry breaking. The other authors focused more on the mechanism itself. Higgs focused on the physical particle the mechanism implied. The Nobel Prize in physics in 2013 was awarded to Peter Higgs and Francois Englett who by that time was the sole surviving member of the boutlet collaboration. Robert Bout having passed away in 2011. Gerald Geralnik, Carl Hagen, and Tom Kibble were not included. a decision that remains controversial in the physics community. The Nobel Prize is limited to three recipients and six people independently contributed to the discovery of the mechanism. What makes the story remarkable is that none of these physicists expected to wait 48 years for experimental confirmation. When the papers were published in 1964, the electroeak theory itself did not yet exist in its modern form. Steven Weineberg and Abdus Salum independently developed the electroeak theory in 1967 and 1968 incorporating the bouting Higs mechanism as its central component. Gerard Huft and Martineis Veltman proved in 1971 that the electroeak theory was mathematically consistent, that it was what physicists call reormalizable. Without reormalizability, the theory would give infinite answers to physical questions and would be useless for calculation. With it, the theory became predictive in an extraordinary way. The discovery of the W and Z bzons at CERN in 1983 was the first major triumph of the electroeak theory. The masses predicted about 80 and 91 Gev were confirmed with remarkable precision. At that point the existence of the Higs Boson was not in serious doubt. The only question was its mass and the search for it took another 30 years. That search required building the large electron posetron collider at CERN in the 1980s which searched up to a Higs mass of about 114 GEV without finding it. Then the Teatron at Fermy Lab which searched higher still without a definitive discovery. Then the LHC which was specifically designed to guarantee discovery of the Higs regardless of its mass. The logic was simple. The LHC runs at energies high enough to produce Higs Bzons in any mass range up to about one te. If the Higs exists and has a mass in that range, the LHC would find it. Either you find the Higs or you find something else that is doing the job of the Higs because something must be electroeak symmetry must be broken. The W and Z bosons are massive. Whatever is causing that must show up. The LHC was designed as a machine for answering this question once and for all. and it did in 2012 with a mass of 125.25 GEV, sitting at the bottom of the allowed mass range, lighter than most theorists had expected and lighter in a way that would prove to be significant because a lighter Higs means a longer lived vacuum. But a lighter Higs also means a smaller hierarchy problem in absolute terms even as it persists in relative terms. And a lighter Higs means that the couplings to certain particles like the bottom quark and the tow lepton are smaller and harder to measure making the precision program more demanding. The universe chose the specific Higs mass that is hardest to study in certain ways and that sits precisely at the stability edge of the vacuum. It is almost provocative. There is one final aspect of the Higs question that connects to the very beginning of physics. The ancient question of what matter is made of. The Greek philosophers proposed atoms, indivisible units of matter from which everything is built. Modern physics replaced those atoms with electrons, protons and neutrons and then replace those with quarks and lepttons and force carriers. And now we have the standard model with its 16 fundamental particles and the Higs. Each time we thought we had reached the bottom, we found another layer. The word atom itself, from the Greek for uncutable, turned out to be misnamed. Atoms are divisible into nucleus and electrons. The nucleus is divisible into protons and neutrons. The proton is divisible into quarks. Are quarks divisible? Is the electron divisible? Is the higs boson divisible? We don't know. The current experimental evidence says that if there is internal structure, it is at a scale below what our best instruments can resolve. Quarks and electrons look pointlike to the precision of current experiments. But so did atoms before the experiments that revealed nuclear structure. So did protons before the experiments that revealed quark structure. The pattern is consistent and sobering. Every generation believed it had reached the bottom. Every generation was wrong. The question is not whether the pattern will repeat. The pattern has repeated too many times to dismiss. The question is when and with what machines and with what theoretical insight to interpret what the machines find. The Higs Bosan stands at the center of the current generation's attempt to go deeper. It is the place where the standard model is most vulnerable, where theory is most clearly incomplete, where the gap between what we know and what we need to know is widest. And that makes it the most interesting place in all of physics. The most interesting particle we have ever found. Not the most exotic, not the most energetic, but the most theoretically fraught. The one that carries the most unanswered questions. The one that when finally understood will tell us the most. And that is what makes it unlike any particle physicists have ever studied before. Every other fundamental particle either slots cleanly into a known category or behaves as theory predicted. The Higs does neither. It sits at the intersection of everything we understand and everything we don't. The Higs Bzon is not finished with us. We found it. We confirmed it exists. We measured its basic properties. And then it handed us back a list of questions longer than the one we started with. That is what a truly significant discovery does. It does not close chapters. It opens them. The hierarchy problem, the question of naturalness, the nature of electroeak symmetry breaking, the matter antimatter asymmetry, the origin of dark matter, the stability of the vacuum. All of these connect to the Higs. All of these are unanswered. And the question of what the Higs is made of sits at the intersection of all of them. Understanding the structure of the Higs or confirming that it has no structure will not answer all of these questions. But it will constrain the answers dramatically. It will tell us which theoretical frameworks are right and which are wrong, which machines to build next, which ideas to pursue, the answer to one question becoming the compass for the next generation of questions. That is how science advances, not in straight lines, in spirals. Each revolution bringing you closer to something that keeps receding as you approach it. And yet you approach it. Each measurement more precise than the last. Each machine more powerful than the one before. Each generation of physicists inheriting a richer set of tools and a narrower set of mysteries. The Higs Bzon is the current center of that spiral and we are turning. Whatever the Higs Bzon turns out to be, the act of asking what it is made of is itself significant. It is a refusal to accept the catalog. A refusal to write in the free parameters without asking why. A refusal to call something fundamental without checking. That refusal is the engine of physics. It is what drove the experiments at Stanford. It is what drove the construction of the LHC. It is what drives the planning of everything that comes next. The question is alive. The machines are running and the universe as it always has will answer in its own time in its own way with exactly the kind of surprise that makes every answer worth waiting for. Good night.
fullTextVi: Tối nay, chúng ta sẽ đi vào bên trong vật thể nhỏ nhất mà các nhà vật lý từng tìm thấy và hỏi một câu hỏi mà hầu như không ai nghĩ tới để hỏi. Không phải Higs Bzon làm gì và nó đến từ đâu, mà là nó thực sự được làm bằng Bởi vì đây là điều mà hầu hết mọi người không nhận ra. Higs Bzon, hạt được cho là mang lại khối lượng cho mọi thứ trong vũ trụ, hạt phải mất 50 năm và là cỗ máy lớn nhất từng được chế tạo để tìm có thể không cơ bản chút nào. Nó có thể có cấu trúc. Nó có thể có các bộ phận. Và nếu đúng như vậy, mọi thứ chúng ta nghĩ là chúng ta biết về lý do tại sao vật chất tồn tại, tại sao bạn tồn tại, cần được xây dựng lại từ đầu. Đến cuối đêm nay, bạn sẽ không chỉ hiểu hạt Higs là gì Bzon là vậy, nhưng tại sao câu hỏi nó được làm từ gì lại có thể là câu hỏi quan trọng nhất trong toàn bộ vật lý. Trước khi chúng ta bắt đầu, nếu bạn cũng thích những chủ đề này như chúng tôi, hãy tạo chắc chắn sẽ thích video hoặc đăng ký. Đó là một hành động đơn giản nhưng nó giúp kênh này tiếp cận được nhiều bộ óc tò mò hơn như của bạn. Bây giờ, hãy bắt đầu. Có một trường lấp đầy tất cả không gian. Mỗi cm khối của vũ trụ, từ khoảng trống rỗng nhất giữa các thiên hà cho đến bên trong cơ thể bạn, được xuyên qua bởi thứ gì đó vô hình. Bạn không thể nhìn thấy nó. Bạn không thể cảm nhận nó một cách trực tiếp. Không có dụng cụ nào có thể chỉ vào nó và nói: "Nó đây. " Nhưng không có nó, không có gì có khối lượng. Electron, quark, các khối cấu tạo nên mọi nguyên tử trong mọi ngôi sao trong mọi thiên hà sẽ hoàn toàn không có khối lượng. Họ sẽ chạy xuyên vũ trụ với tốc độ ánh sáng, không bao giờ chậm lại, không bao giờ liên kết với nhau, không bao giờ tạo thành những cấu trúc mà chúng ta gọi là vật chất. Sẽ không có nguyên tử, không có phân tử, không có hóa học, không có hành tinh, không có bạn. Trường này được gọi là trường Higs và nó ở dạng rất thực tế cảm nhận lý do mọi thứ tồn tại theo cách nó tồn tại. Higs Bzon là cái mà các nhà vật lý gọi là sự kích thích của trường đó. Khi bạn đổ đủ năng lượng vào trường Higs trong một vùng đủ nhỏ của không gian, bạn quấy rối nó. Và sự xáo trộn đó có dạng một hạt, một gợn sóng trong thứ gì đó mặt khác thì hoàn toàn tĩnh lặng. Hạt đó là Higs Bzon. Và vào ngày 4 tháng 7 năm 2012, sau khi tìm kiếm nó gần 50 nhiều năm, các nhà vật lý đã tìm thấy nó. Thông báo đến từ CERN, Tổ chức Nghiên cứu Hạt nhân Châu Âu ở Thụy Sĩ Biên giới Pháp bên ngoài Geneva. Cả hai nhóm hợp tác máy dò lớn tại Máy Va chạm Hadron Lớn, Atlas và CMS, đã công bố khám phá đồng thời. Đó là một trong những khoảnh khắc quan trọng nhất trong lịch sử khoa học. Đám đông trong khán phòng bao gồm chính Peter Higgs, nhà vật lý người Anh, người đã lần đầu tiên đề xuất cơ chế này vào năm 1964. Ông đã 83 tuổi. Khi kết quả được công bố, người ta thấy anh ấy đang lau nước mắt. Ông đã dành gần nửa thế kỷ để chờ đợi sự xác nhận này. Nhưng đây là lúc câu chuyện trở nên phức tạp. Việc phát hiện ra Higs Bzon không phải là sự kết thúc của một điều gì đó. Đó là sự khởi đầu của một loạt câu hỏi hoàn toàn khác. Bởi vì vào thời điểm các nhà vật lý thực sự có Higs Bzon để nghiên cứu, họ bắt đầu đo it. Khối lượng của nó, spin của nó, cách nó phân hủy thành các hạt khác, tốc độ những phân rã đó xảy ra. Và một số phép đo đó đã cho kết quả gần như chính xác, gần như chính xác như dự đoán, gần như, nhưng không hoàn toàn. Và trong vật lý, gần như là một từ rất thú vị. Mô hình chuẩn của vật lý hạt là lý thuyết khoa học thành công nhất từng được viết ra down. Nó mô tả với độ chính xác phi thường hành vi của tất cả các hạt cơ bản đã biết và các lực lượng cai trị chúng với một ngoại lệ chính mà chúng ta sẽ quay lại. Nó dự đoán sự tồn tại của các hạt hàng thập kỷ trước khi các thí nghiệm có thể tìm thấy chúng. Nó đưa ra những dự đoán bằng số chính xác đến hơn 10 chữ số thập phân. Khi lý thuyết cho rằng mômen từ của electron phải bằng 2. 0 2319 30 436 và bạn đo nó và lấy chính xác số đó, bạn bắt đầu tin vào lý thuyết. Mô hình chuẩn được xây dựng trên một khuôn khổ gọi là lý thuyết trường lượng tử. Ý tưởng cơ bản là không gian không trống rỗng. Nó chứa đầy các lĩnh vực. Mỗi loại hạt tương ứng với một trường thấm vào toàn bộ không gian. Electron là sự kích thích của trường electron. Photon là sự kích thích của trường điện từ. Quark là sự kích thích của trường quark. Và Higs Bzon là sự kích thích của trường Higs. Các trường này tương tác với nhau theo các quy tắc có thể được viết ra như các phương trình toán học chính xác. Các tương tác tạo ra những gì chúng ta quan sát thấy là lực. Lực điện từ, lực hạt nhân yếu, lực hạt nhân mạnh. Mô hình tiêu chuẩn mô tả tất cả những điều này một cách tuyệt vời. Nó không mô tả trọng lực. Đó là ngoại lệ. Thuyết tương đối rộng xử lý lực hấp dẫn và hai khuôn khổ lý thuyết trường lượng tử và thuyết tương đối rộng cho đến nay vẫn từ chối thống nhất thành một mô tả nhất quán duy nhất. Vấn đề đó là có thật, to lớn và tách biệt khỏi những gì chúng ta đang thảo luận ở đây. Nhưng trong phạm vi của nó, mô hình chuẩn là một cỗ máy hoạt động đơn giản. Trường Higs chiếm một vị trí độc nhất trong đó. Các trường khác trong mô hình chuẩn có được các thuộc tính của chúng từ toán học của lý thuyết. Photon không có khối lượng do tính đối xứng trong các phương trình. Gluon không có khối lượng vì một lý do liên quan, nhưng trường Higs thì khác. Trường Higs có cái gọi là giá trị kỳ vọng chân không khác 0. Đó là một cụm từ kỹ thuật có ý nghĩa rất cụ thể. Nó có nghĩa là ngay cả ở trạng thái năng lượng thấp nhất, ngay cả khi vũ trụ Bình tĩnh và trống rỗng nhất có thể, Higsfield không ngồi ở zero. Nó nằm ở một giá trị cụ thể khác 0, giống như một quả bóng ở đầu một ngọn đồi đối xứng hoàn hảo đã lăn sang một bên và ổn định ở đó. Giá trị chính xác mà nó đạt được là 246 ga electron volt. Vì vậy, bạn không bao giờ nhìn thấy trực tiếp Higs Bzon. Bạn nhìn thấy các hạt nó phân hủy thành. Và sau đó bạn đi ngược lại để phát hiện ra rằng Higs Bzon đã ở đó. Higs có một số dạng phân rã chính. Phổ biến nhất khoảng 58% thời gian là phân rã thành một cặp quark đáy. Quark đáy và phản hạt của nó được tạo ra cùng nhau. Kênh phân rã quark đáy chỉ được quan sát thấy có ý nghĩa quan trọng vào năm 2018, 6 năm sau phát hiện đầu tiên. Phân rã phổ biến thứ hai khoảng 22% thời gian là thành một cặp của boson W. Nhưng một trong những boson W nằm ngoài vỏ, nghĩa là nó không có đủ năng lượng là một boson W thực sự. Điều này làm cho việc tái thiết trở nên phức tạp. Đây là những tín hiệu sạch sẽ trong máy dò, dễ nhận biết. Rất hiếm, nhưng các photon được đo rất chính xác trong máy dò. Kênh phân rã hai photon là một trong hai kênh chính của khám phá ban đầu. Mỗi chế độ phân rã này đều nhạy cảm với các khía cạnh khác nhau của sự ghép nối Higs. Sự phân rã thành quark đáy đo lường sự liên kết với quark đáy. Sự phân rã thành bosan W đo lường sự liên kết với boson W. Sự phân rã thành hai photon bao gồm các vòng quark top và W bzon. Vì vậy, nó cũng nhạy cảm với sự kết hợp với các quark đỉnh. segments.viText: Hạt thú vị nhất mà chúng tôi từng tìm thấy.

segments.text: Not the most exotic, not the most energetic, but the most theoretically fraught.
segments.viText: Không phải là điều kỳ lạ nhất, không phải là điều mạnh mẽ nhất, nhưng là điều khó khăn nhất về mặt lý thuyết.

segments.text: The one that carries the most unanswered questions.
segments.viText: Một trong những câu hỏi chưa được trả lời nhất.

segments.text: The one that when finally understood will tell us the most.
segments.viText: Điều mà cuối cùng khi hiểu được sẽ cho chúng ta biết nhiều nhất.

segments.text: And that is what makes it unlike any particle physicists have ever studied before.
segments.viText: Và đó là điều khiến nó không giống bất kỳ nhà vật lý hạt nào từng nghiên cứu trước đây.

segments.text: Every other fundamental particle either slots cleanly into a known category or behaves as
segments.viText: Mọi hạt cơ bản khác đều được sắp xếp rõ ràng vào một danh mục đã biết hoặc hoạt động như

segments.text: theory predicted.
segments.viText: lý thuyết dự đoán.

segments.text: The Higs does neither.
segments.viText: Higs cũng không làm như vậy.

segments.text: It sits at the intersection of everything we understand and everything we don't.
segments.viText: Nó nằm ở giao điểm của mọi thứ chúng ta hiểu và mọi thứ chúng ta không hiểu.

segments.text: The Higs Bzon is not finished with us.
segments.viText: Higs Bzon vẫn chưa kết thúc với chúng tôi.

segments.text: We found it.
segments.viText: Chúng tôi đã tìm thấy nó.

segments.text: We confirmed it exists.
segments.viText: Chúng tôi xác nhận nó tồn tại.

segments.text: We measured its basic properties.
segments.viText: Chúng tôi đã đo các đặc tính cơ bản của nó.

segments.text: And then it handed us back a list of questions longer than the one
segments.viText: Và sau đó nó đưa lại cho chúng tôi một danh sách các câu hỏi dài hơn danh sách

segments.text: we started with.
segments.viText: chúng tôi đã bắt đầu với

segments.text: That is what a truly significant discovery does.
segments.viText: Đó chính là điều mà một khám phá thực sự quan trọng mang lại.

segments.text: It does not close chapters.
segments.viText: Nó không đóng chương.

segments.text: It opens them.
segments.viText: Nó mở chúng ra.

segments.text: The hierarchy problem, the question of naturalness, the nature of electroeak symmetry breaking, the
segments.viText: Bài toán thứ bậc, câu hỏi về tính tự nhiên, bản chất của sự phá vỡ đối xứng điện cực,

segments.text: matter antimatter asymmetry, the origin of dark matter, the stability of the vacuum.
segments.viText: sự bất đối xứng của vật chất phản vật chất, nguồn gốc của vật chất tối, tính ổn định của chân không.

segments.text: All of these connect to the Higs.
segments.viText: Tất cả những thứ này đều kết nối với Higs.

segments.text: All of these are unanswered.
segments.viText: Tất cả những điều này đều chưa được trả lời.

segments.text: And the question of what the Higs is made of sits at the intersection
segments.viText: Và câu hỏi Higs được làm từ gì nằm ở giao điểm

segments.text: of all of them.
segments.viText: của tất cả chúng.

segments.text: Understanding the structure of the Higs or confirming that it has no structure will
segments.viText: Hiểu được cấu trúc của Higs hoặc xác nhận rằng nó không có cấu trúc sẽ

segments.text: not answer all of these questions.
segments.viText: không trả lời được tất cả những câu hỏi này.

segments.text: But it will constrain the answers dramatically.
segments.viText: Nhưng nó sẽ hạn chế đáng kể các câu trả lời.

segments.text: It will tell us which theoretical frameworks are right and which are wrong, which
segments.viText: Nó sẽ cho chúng ta biết khuôn khổ lý thuyết nào đúng, khuôn khổ lý thuyết nào sai,

segments.text: machines to build next, which ideas to pursue, the answer to one question becoming
segments.viText: tiếp theo nên chế tạo những cỗ máy nào, theo đuổi ý tưởng nào, câu trả lời cho một câu hỏi sẽ trở thành

segments.text: the compass for the next generation of questions.
segments.viText: la bàn cho thế hệ câu hỏi tiếp theo.

segments.text: That is how science advances, not in straight lines, in spirals.
segments.viText: Đó là cách khoa học tiến bộ, không phải theo đường thẳng mà theo hình xoắn ốc.

segments.text: Each revolution bringing you closer to something that keeps receding as you approach it.
segments.viText: Mỗi cuộc cách mạng đưa bạn đến gần hơn với một thứ gì đó luôn lùi xa khi bạn tiếp cận nó.

segments.text: And yet you approach it.
segments.viText: Tuy nhiên, bạn tiếp cận nó.

segments.text: Each measurement more precise than the last.
segments.viText: Mỗi phép đo chính xác hơn lần trước.

segments.text: Each machine more powerful than the one before.
segments.viText: Mỗi máy mạnh hơn máy trước.

segments.text: Each generation of physicists inheriting a richer set of tools and a narrower set
segments.viText: Mỗi thế hệ nhà vật lý kế thừa một bộ công cụ phong phú hơn và một bộ công cụ hẹp hơn

segments.text: of mysteries.
segments.viText: của những điều bí ẩn.

segments.text: The Higs Bzon is the current center of that spiral and we are turning.
segments.viText: Higs Bzon là trung tâm hiện tại của đường xoắn ốc đó và chúng ta đang quay.

segments.text: Whatever the Higs Bzon turns out to be, the act of asking what it
segments.viText: Dù Higs Bzon hóa ra là gì thì hành động hỏi nó là gì

segments.text: is made of is itself significant.
segments.viText: được làm bằng chính nó là có ý nghĩa.

segments.text: It is a refusal to accept the catalog.
segments.viText: Đó là sự từ chối chấp nhận danh mục.

segments.text: A refusal to write in the free parameters without asking why.
segments.viText: Từ chối viết các tham số miễn phí mà không hỏi tại sao.

segments.text: A refusal to call something fundamental without checking.
segments.viText: Từ chối gọi điều gì đó là cơ bản mà không kiểm tra.

segments.text: That refusal is the engine of physics.
segments.viText: Sự từ chối đó là động cơ của vật lý.

segments.text: It is what drove the experiments at Stanford.
segments.viText: Đó là điều đã thúc đẩy các thí nghiệm ở Stanford.

segments.text: It is what drove the construction of the LHC.
segments.viText: Đó là động lực thúc đẩy việc xây dựng LHC.

segments.text: It is what drives the planning of everything that comes next.
segments.viText: Đó là điều thúc đẩy việc lập kế hoạch cho mọi việc tiếp theo.

segments.text: The question is alive.
segments.viText: Câu hỏi vẫn còn sống.

segments.text: The machines are running and the universe as it always has will answer in
segments.viText: Những cỗ máy đang chạy và vũ trụ như nó luôn có sẽ trả lời trong

segments.text: its own time in its own way with exactly the kind of surprise that
segments.viText: thời gian của riêng nó theo cách riêng của nó với chính xác sự ngạc nhiên

segments.text: makes every answer worth waiting for.
segments.viText: khiến mọi câu trả lời đều đáng để chờ đợi.

segments.text: Good night.
segments.viText: Chúc ngủ ngon.
